title: Capstone Step 1: Choose, Load and Audit a Public Dataset

slide.title: Choose Your Real Dataset
slide.body: Magnifying glass over a data table; a small tag labelled 'Licence ✓' and a clipboard labelled 'Audit'. Small tag: Python for AI · Lesson 19 · Capstone.

production_notes: [VERIFY] Licence terms of World Bank Open Data, Our World in Data, the UCI Machine Learning Repository and Kaggle datasets (Kaggle licences vary per dataset, and Kaggle needs a free account). The voiceover names the four sources only as places to browse and tells learners to check each licence on the dataset's own page; it makes no claim about any licence.
[VERSION] Uploading files through the Colab file panel must be checked against the live interface before recording.

Yusuf's question is hypothetical; no dataset or result is claimed. Screen scenes use a placeholder file name (file_name.csv) and do not show a real dataset's contents or findings. If the team wants to show a real file, pick one whose licence has been checked and add it to these notes.

The audit function demo runs on the synthetic order data from L14. Printed output must match content.md: 'Shape: (11, 8) / Duplicate rows: 1 / Missing values: / order_date 1 / payment 1 / dtype: int64 / Text columns: ['city', 'order_date', 'unit_price', 'payment', 'returned']'.
Stock footage of farms or fields must show no readable brand names or logos.

Hook.voiceover: Until now, you have worked with small practice tables. Real public datasets are bigger, messier, and more interesting. In this lesson, you choose one, ask your own question about it, and find out what condition it is in.

Explain.voiceover: Last time, we built an ML-ready table. Now it is time for your capstone. It is a notebook that takes a real public dataset from raw file to an ML-ready table. It has two steps. Today, you choose, load and audit. In the next lesson, you clean, explore and document.

slide.title: Your capstone
slide.body: Two steps: L19 Choose · Load · Audit → L20 Clean · Explore · Document → ML-ready table.

Explain.voiceover: A good first dataset has a clear question you care about, and a manageable size, from a few hundred to a few hundred thousand rows. It comes as a table, with one row per example. It has a clear licence and a named source. And it has some imperfections, or there is nothing to audit.

slide.title: A good first dataset
slide.body: Clear question · A few hundred to a few hundred thousand rows, 5 to 30 columns · Table format, one row per example · Clear licence and source · Some imperfections

Explain.voiceover: Good places to browse include World Bank Open Data, Our World in Data, the UCI Machine Learning Repository, and Kaggle. Licences differ between sites and between datasets, so always read the licence on the dataset's own page, and write it in your notebook.

slide.title: Where to look
slide.body: World Bank Open Data · Our World in Data · UCI Machine Learning Repository · Kaggle (free account). Read each dataset's licence and record it.

Explain.voiceover: Also check that the data contains no personal information about people who can be identified. If it does, choose another dataset. And never upload personal or confidential data from your job into Colab, or into any AI tool.

Choosing a dataset is like choosing a used car. You check the papers first, the licence and the source. Then you look under the bonnet, which is the audit, before you drive anywhere. A few scratches are fine, if you know where they are. But a car with no papers is a risk, however good it looks.
Explain.on_screen_text: Check the papers, then the engine

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's set up a capstone notebook. Yusuf is an agricultural extension officer in Kampala, Uganda. His question, which is just an example, is this. In countries with similar rainfall, is fertiliser use linked to cereal yield?
Demonstrate.stock_query: farmer and advisor in green field

Demonstrate.voiceover: He creates a new notebook and adds five text headings, in order. Question, Source, Load, Audit, and Cleaning log. The cleaning log stays empty until the next lesson. Under Source, he records the name, the web address, the download date and the licence.
screen_steps: Create a new Colab notebook named: Capstone - cereal yield
Add five text cells with the headings: 1 Question · 2 Source · 3 Load · 4 Audit · 5 Cleaning log
Under Source, type placeholders: Name · Web address · Download date · Licence

Demonstrate.voiceover: Then he uploads the downloaded file with the Colab file panel, loads it with read csv, and takes a first look with head and info.
screen_steps: Open the Colab file panel and upload the downloaded CSV
Under Load, type: df = pd.read_csv("file_name.csv")
Type: df.head() and df.info() in separate cells

Demonstrate.voiceover: Next, he writes a reusable audit function, so he can run the same checks again after cleaning. It prints the shape, the number of duplicate rows, the missing values in each column that has some, and the list of text columns.
screen_steps: Under Audit, add a code cell
Type: def audit(df):
Type (indented): """Print a short data-quality report for a DataFrame."""
Type (indented): print("Shape:", df.shape) / print("Duplicate rows:", df.duplicated().sum())
Type (indented): print("Missing values:") / print(df.isna().sum()[lambda s: s > 0])
Type (indented): print("Text columns:", df.select_dtypes(exclude="number").columns.tolist())
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Write the audit once, reuse it

Demonstrate.voiceover: To show that it works, we test it on the synthetic order data from lesson fourteen. Eleven rows, one duplicate, a missing date and payment, and five text columns. Exactly what we found by hand.
screen_steps: Run the L14 data cell
Type: audit(orders)
Press Shift + Enter
Output: Shape: (11, 8) / Duplicate rows: 1 / Missing values: order_date 1, payment 1 / Text columns: ['city', 'order_date', 'unit_price', 'payment', 'returned']

Demonstrate.voiceover: On his real data, Yusuf runs the audit, then describe, unique on the category columns, and a quick histogram. He writes each problem in the Audit section, marked as an error or needing a decision.
screen_steps: Type: audit(df), then df.describe()
Type: df["category_column"].unique() for each category column
Plot a histogram of the main number column
In the Audit text cell, list each problem marked 'error' or 'needs a decision'

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is choosing a dataset that is too large or complex, and spending the whole week on loading problems. Before you commit, ask one question. Does this table have a column I can use as a target, and columns that could explain it? If not, choose again now.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, choose a public dataset with a clear question, a manageable size, a table format, and a licence that allows your use. Second, record the source, download date and licence before any analysis. Third, audit the data with reusable code, and list every problem before you start cleaning.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Clear question, manageable size, table format, usable licence. 2. Record source, date and licence first. 3. Reusable audit code; list every problem.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. This exercise is step one of your capstone. Choose a dataset, write your question, load the data, and complete a full audit in your notebook. Give yourself about forty-five minutes. In the next and final lesson, Capstone Step Two, you clean, explore and document your notebook. See you there.
